ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description first: The attached diagram shows a square at the bottom and a triangle attached along the square’s entire top side. The square’s top horizontal side is the triangle’s base, so that shared side lies inside the combined figure and is not part of the outside perimeter of the irregular pentagon. Reasoning: Let the side length of the square be s. Then the perimeter of the square is 4s. The problem states that the triangle has the same perimeter as the square, so the triangle perimeter is also 4s. Since the triangle’s base is the shared top side of the square, the base has length s. Therefore, the two exposed slanted sides of the triangle together have length 4s - s = 3s. The outside perimeter of the pentagon consists of the three exposed sides of the square, totaling 3s, plus the two exposed slanted triangle sides, totaling 3s. Thus the pentagon perimeter is 6s. Compared with the square perimeter 4s, the ratio is 6s:4s = 3:2.

method.method_draft: Describe the image first: the square and triangle are joined along one full side, the square’s top edge, making that edge internal to the combined pentagon. Use a union-perimeter approach. Let the square side be s, so the shared edge has length s. From the text, P_triangle = P_square; call this common perimeter 4s because the square has four equal sides. If one adds the separate perimeters of the square and triangle, the shared edge is counted twice, but it disappears from the outside perimeter of the joined pentagon. Therefore P_pentagon = P_square + P_triangle - 2s = 4s + 4s - 2s = 6s. The ratio to the square perimeter is 6s:4s = 3:2.
